source: Polu & Sutskever (2020) Generative Language Modeling for Automated Theorem Proving (GPT-f)
finding: First transformer prover for Metamath. A language model proposes tactics (next proof steps). A best-first search keeps a queue of goals sorted by cumulative log-probability of the tactics that led to them, and the model is called to expand the top goal. A Metamath kernel checks every proof.
numbers: Best model (700M params) closes 56.22% of held-out set.mm test theorems (search e=32 tactics per goal, a=32 attempts, d=256 depth) vs 21.16% for prior state of the art MetaGen-IL. Evaluation cost about 1k V100 GPU-hours per validation run.
quote: capable of closing 56.22% of proofs from a held-out test set (vs 21.16% for the current state of the art, MetaGen-IL)
limits: Metamath proofs are 10-20 steps per goal on average and have no high-level tactics, so results may not transfer. Single formal system. Test set is in-library theorems.
agent_relevance: The template for S3 plus S4: the model only proposes candidate steps, plain code ranks and expands them, and a verifier accepts. Search order is set by program, not by the model.

source: Polu & Sutskever (2020) GPT-f - pretraining, size and value function ablations
finding: Pretraining on math text helps; size helps but saturates; a learned value function on top of the policy helps; more attempts help.
numbers: Validation pass rate: 160M WebMath 34.79%, 400M 39.94%, 700M 42.56%, 1.5B 42.39% (no gain from 700M to 1.5B). Policy-only 700M 42.56% vs policy+value 47.21% (value reranking). Github-only pretraining below WebMath (Github+arXiv+MathStackExchange mix). Raw vs augmented data: 700M 40.28% raw vs higher with augmentation.
limits: Authors say the non-monotone size result may come from a validation set with uneven difficulty or saturation on small training data.
agent_relevance: A value or score over partial states beats raw proposal probability. For a no-training scaffold, the analogue is a cheap program-computed state score, not a model self-rating.

source: Polu & Sutskever (2020) GPT-f - contribution to Metamath library
finding: The prover found shorter proofs than the human ones for existing theorems, and the Metamath community accepted them.
numbers: 23 shortened proofs accepted into set.mm. Community comments called the results impressive given a recent global minimization.
limits: Small count. Proof length is the metric this community cares about, not difficulty.
agent_relevance: Verifier-checked output from a model can beat human work on a narrow metric. Accept by checker, not by trust.

source: Han, Rute, Wu, Ayers, Polu (2021/2022) Proof Artifact Co-Training for Theorem Proving with Language Models (PACT)
finding: Extra self-supervised tasks mined from kernel-level proof terms, trained together with tactic prediction, raise Lean theorem proving. Co-training beats pretraining on the same data. Gains are not mere regularization.
numbers: Pass rate on held-out mathlib theorems rises from 32% (tactic only) to 48.4% (WebMath then mix1+mix2+tactic). A WebMath>tactic model with 15% dropout reached 33.6%, far below 48.4%. On future-mathlib (temporally held-out, 2,800ish theorems): refl baseline 11.6%, tidy-bfs 21.8%, best model 37.1% (1043 proofs). Over one third of found proofs shorter than ground truth; 19 co-authored mathlib commits.
quote: WebMath > tactic model trained with 15% residual dropout achieved ... 33.6% pass rate, far below the 48.4% PACT pass rate
limits: Lean 3 only. Distribution shift cuts success to 37.1% on new library files. Many future-mathlib hits are trivial boilerplate.
agent_relevance: Data richness in the proposer matters, but our scaffold cannot train. What transfers: verify steps with the real checker and keep short, checked proofs.

source: Polu, Han, Zheng, Baksys, Babuschkin, Sutskever (2022) Formal Mathematics Statement Curriculum Learning
finding: Expert iteration: run proof search, keep successful proofs, retrain the model on them, repeat. At equal compute this beats search-only. It finds a curriculum of harder problems without ground-truth proofs.
numbers: mathlib-valid pass@1 56.3% (iteration 1) to 62.6% (iteration 9), roughly logarithmic in iterations. Synthetic inequalities: expert iteration closes 6 problems at difficulty ND=6 with no seed proofs; sample-only loop stays at 0. miniF2F: 47.3% valid (a=64 attempts), 36.6% test; solves 26 AMC12, 6 AIME, 2 IMO-adapted problems. Prior miniF2F-test SOTA about 29.3%.
quote: expert iteration eventually closes proofs of hard statements that remain completely out of reach of simply sampling proof searches without interleaved training
limits: Needs weeks of training compute and 25k+ statements. The 774M model; bigger models gave higher pass@1 but a smaller model with more samples won at fixed compute. Manually formalized 327 curriculum statements were used. Zero-shot transfer from mathlib to miniF2F was initially weak.
agent_relevance: Search attempts alone plateau; the gain comes from learning. Without training, our scaffold may only match 'sample only' unless it stores verified lemmas (O-level memory) in context.

source: Polu et al. (2022) Formal Mathematics Statement Curriculum Learning - test-time compute vs model size
finding: At fixed compute, sampling more proof attempts from a smaller model can beat a larger model. Cumulative pass@16k from repeated sampling saturates well below expert-iterated models.
numbers: Single model size 774M used. Pass@1 and pass@8 curves reported over 8 iterations; cumulative pass rate on miniF2F-valid reached 47.3% with a=64 vs about 41.2-44.1% at lower attempts.
quote: for a fixed amount of compute, sampling more attempts from a smaller model leads to a better final performance
limits: Authors say size scaling is not as clean as in unsupervised LM scaling; experiments with other sizes not reported.
agent_relevance: For a frozen model, budget goes to more checked attempts, not bigger single thoughts. This supports breadth with a hard verifier.

source: Lample, Lachaux, Lavril et al. (2022) HyperTree Proof Search for Neural Theorem Proving (HTPS)
finding: AlphaZero-style search over a hypergraph because one tactic can create several subgoals that all must be solved (AND-OR structure). Policy and value are one transformer, trained online from its own proof searches.
numbers: miniF2F-test 41.0% pass@64 vs 36.6% for GPT-f; without the synthetic co-training task 38.5% test. miniF2F-valid cumulative 58.6% (54.9% without synthetic task). Metamath: online training lifts held-out valid from 61% pass@8 to 82.6% cumulative, and test pass@32 from 55.8% to 65.6%; supervised model alone gets 65.4% valid and 61.2% test vs GPT-f 56.5% and 56.2%.
limits: Part of the valid gain comes from training on valid statements themselves (they said the gain is not only that; ablation vs supervised model with same attempts). Huge distributed compute (days of training).
agent_relevance: Proofs need AND-OR bookkeeping: a node is solved only when all children are. Our S3/S4 loop should track subgoal sets in code, not in model text.

source: Jiang, Li, Tworkowski et al. (2022) Thor: Wielding Hammers to Integrate Language Models and Automated Theorem Provers
finding: Split the work: a language model plans steps and emits a special hammer token when it thinks a symbolic prover can finish; a hammer (Sledgehammer) does premise selection and closes the goal. The hybrid solves problems neither can alone.
numbers: PISA success rate 39.0% (LM alone) to 57.0% (Thor); 8.2% of problems solved that neither LM nor Sledgehammer solve alone. miniF2F-test 29.9% vs 29.6% for GPT-f expert iteration with far less compute. LM steps with premises advance proof only 1.9% of the time vs 28.2% for steps without premises. Preprocessing cost estimated at 7,400 CPU hours per year of AFP.
quote: Hence, a good mechanism for premise selection could bring crucial benefits.
limits: Isabelle-specific; PISA numbers do not carry to Lean. 1.9% vs 28.2% is an observational comparison, not a controlled one.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence for tool handoff: the model decides WHEN to call a solver, code runs the solver. Matches the 'program decides, model fills a slot' rule.

source: Jiang, Welleck, Zhou et al. (2023) Draft, Sketch, and Prove (DSP)
finding: Use an informal proof to draft a formal sketch (with gaps), then let automated provers fill each gap. The LM plans at the sketch level; the symbolic tool closes small steps.
numbers: miniF2F-test Isabelle: Sledgehammer 10.4%, Sledgehammer+heuristics 20.9%, Thor 29.9%, Thor+expert iteration 35.2%; DSP with human informal proofs 39.3% test, 42.6% valid (Codex informal 40.6% valid / 35.3% test; 540B Minerva 42.6% valid / 38.9% test). Ablations (valid): no in-line comments 37.7% (-4.9), no informal proofs 38.9% (-3.7), no automated provers 32.8% (-9.8). Test: 36.5, 34.0, 30.3.
limits: Pass counts are with many sketch attempts (100 informal proofs, many sketches). Only algebra and number theory examples were hand written (20 demos). Codex-generated informal proofs sometimes match human ones, so informal quality is not the bottleneck.
agent_relevance: Informal draft then verified formal fill is a ready S3 pattern. Biggest drop comes from removing the tool, not the informal text.

source: Yang, Swope, Gu et al. (2023) LeanDojo: Theorem Proving with Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
finding: Open Lean toolkit and benchmark, plus ReProver, a retrieval-augmented tactic generator. Random train/test splits overstate performance because of memorization; a novel_premises split exposes this.
numbers: 98,734 theorems; split 94,734/2,000/2,000. Pass@1 random split: tidy 23.8, GPT-4 zero-shot 29.0, ReProver w/o retrieval 47.6, ReProver 51.2. novel_premises split: tidy 5.3, GPT-4 7.4, ReProver w/o retrieval 23.2, ReProver 26.3. miniF2F-test 26.5% pass@1; ProofNet 13.8%. Found 33 new proofs on miniF2F and 39 on ProofNet. LeanDojo cuts false proof-check errors from 21.1% to 1.4%. Training 5 days on one GPU.
quote: the common practice of splitting theorems randomly into training/testing has led to an overestimated performance in the previous papers
limits: Pass@1 under a time limit; GPT-4 may have seen proofs (contamination), so 29.0% is not a clean number. Retrieval gain is much smaller on novel_premises (23.2 to 26.3).
agent_relevance: Warns that benchmark numbers need leakage-safe splits. Also shows checker plumbing errors (21.1% false rejects) can swamp the signal; verifier reliability is part of the loop.

source: Thakur, Tsoukalas, Wen, Xin, Chaudhuri (2024) An In-Context Learning Agent for Formal Theorem-Proving (COPRA)
finding: No fine-tuning. GPT-4 proposes one tactic at a time inside a program-controlled backtracking search. Proof-assistant error messages, search history and retrieved lemmas go back into the prompt. Few-shot whole-proof prompting works poorly.
numbers: miniF2F-test (Lean) COPRA with GPT-4 solves 29.09% at pass@1, above ReProver 26.5% and Llemma; query cap 60 per problem. Table 1 few-shot baselines: CodeLlama 0.0%, GPT-3.5 2.8%, COPRA(CodeLlama) 5.73%, COPRA(GPT-3.5) 9.02%, few-shot GPT-4 13.52%; COPRA(GPT-4) more than twice few-shot GPT-4. Backtracking helps most on long proofs.
quote: few-shot prompting of GPT-4 is not effective at proof generation
limits: Possible GPT-4 test-set memorization (authors raise it). Query count, not wall time, is the budget. Weaker base models gain little, so the scaffold needs a strong model.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to our target: frozen LLM, program-owned search, real checker feedback in the next prompt. Directly supports G2 (revise from real output).

source: Xin, Guo, Shao et al. (2024) DeepSeek-Prover: Advancing Theorem Proving in LLMs through Large-Scale Synthetic Data
finding: Auto-formalize informal competition problems into Lean 4 statements, filter easy or invalid ones, generate proofs, keep Lean-verified ones, retrain, repeat. Whole-proof generation without search.
numbers: About 8 million synthesized formal statements with proofs. DeepSeekMath-7B base reaches 46.3% on miniF2F-test whole-proof at 64 samples, cumulative 52.0% test and 60.2% valid; GPT-4 25.41% valid and 22.95% test; HTPS 58.6% valid and 41.0% test. Also 148 FIMO problems tested.
limits: Test-time budget large (cumulative over many samples). Synthetic statements may be easier than real ones; quality filter and hypothesis rejection were needed.
agent_relevance: Shows verified self-generated data beats scarce human data when the checker is exact. Not usable without training.

source: Xin, Ren, Song et al. (2024) DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5: Harnessing Proof Assistant Feedback for RL and Monte-Carlo Tree Search
finding: Combines whole-proof generation with a truncate-and-resume tree search (RMaxTS, an exploration-reward MCTS). Keep the successful prefix of a generated proof, parse it into tactic nodes, and resume generation from the last good tactic state. RL (GRPO) on Lean verifier feedback.
numbers: miniF2F-test single-pass 60.2% for RL model vs 50.0% for V1; at 128 samples 51.6% (rows with 46.1, 50.0, 50.7, 51.6, 54.9, 58.4 across budgets); with RMaxTS 63.5%. ProofNet: 22.6% single pass, 25.3% with RMaxTS, vs ReProver 13.8% and InternLM2-StepProver 18.1%. Intrinsic reward: sparse extrinsic reward only at full proof, so RMaxTS adds a curiosity bonus.
quote: the search agent only obtains non-zero rewards when the proof is completely solved
limits: Tree search adds only about 3.3 points over single pass at very large budgets. Budgets are matched by samples, not wall time.
agent_relevance: Truncate-and-resume is a concrete S3-S4 operator: keep the verified prefix, regenerate the failing tail. Cheap for a frozen model with a checker.

source: Ren, Shao, Song et al. (2025) DeepSeek-Prover-V2: Reinforcement Learning for Subgoal Decomposition
finding: A general LLM (DeepSeek-V3) decomposes a hard theorem into subgoals written as Lean 'sorry' lemmas; a 7B prover solves each subgoal; solved subgoals are stitched into a chain-of-thought plus proof for cold-start training. RL follows. Planning in language, verification in Lean.
numbers: 671B model: miniF2F-test 82.4% at pass@32 and 88.9% at pass@8192; ProofNet-test 37.1% at pass@1024; 47 of 658 PutnamBench problems. New ProverBench of 325 problems (15 from AIME 24 and 25).
limits: Very large budgets (pass@8192). PutnamBench 47/658 (7%) shows the college-level gap. miniF2F is high-school level and likely saturating.
agent_relevance: Decompose then solve pieces separately is the strongest recent recipe; a scaffold can do the decomposition step in language and send pieces to a checker.

source: Lin, Tang, Wang et al. (2025) Goedel-Prover: A Frontier Model for Open-Source Automated Theorem Proving
finding: Expert iteration for 8 rounds on formalized Numina statements, whole-proof generation. Beats DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5-RL at every sampling budget.
numbers: miniF2F pass@32 57.6% vs 50.0% for DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5-RL (+7.6). Solves 7 PutnamBench problems at pass@512 (one initial solve withdrawn after a mis-formalization was found). Solves 29.7K Lean Workbook problems, more than prior open models.
quote: discovered that one of the problems was mis-formalized
limits: Mis-formalized statements can yield false 'solves', so success on a formal statement is not success on the intended problem.
agent_relevance: G3 analogue: a checker passes the statement you formalized, not the one you meant. Keep a check on the statement itself.

source: Wang, Unsal, Lin et al. (2025) Kimina-Prover Preview: Towards Large Formal Reasoning Models with Reinforcement Learning
finding: Large reasoning model in Lean: a think block that mixes informal reasoning with Lean snippets, then a proof. No tree search. Longer thinking correlates with higher pass rates.
numbers: miniF2F-test 80.74% at pass@8192 vs 72.95% for BFS-Prover (prior best among search systems); 52.94% pass@1 and 68.85% pass@32. Trained from Qwen2.5-72B with RL; cold start data from Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking blocks.
limits: Synthetic cold-start reflections were low quality (repetition) until mixed with informal thinking data. 8192 samples is a large budget.
agent_relevance: Shows a reasoning model can replace explicit tree search once trained. Without training, we get the search back through program-controlled retries.

source: Hubert, Mehta, Sartran et al. (2025) Olympiad-level formal mathematical reasoning with reinforcement learning (AlphaProof), Nature
finding: AlphaZero-style agent for Lean: a proof network gives a tactic list and a value; tree search over an AND-OR proof tree; trained by RL on about 80 million auto-formalized Lean problems (from about 1 million natural-language problems). Each statement is attempted for proof or disproof. For hard problems, test-time RL (TTRL) trains on synthetic variants of the target.
numbers: Main RL about 80,000 TPU-days. SFT start: about 300,000 state-tactic pairs from Mathlib. miniF2F-test / formal-imo / PutnamBench: 2 TPU-min 96.3% / 33.2% / 27.9%; 12 TPU-hours 97.7 / 43.7 / 39.4; TTRL 50 TPU-days 97.5 / 53.9 / 45.5; TTRL 500 TPU-days 99.6 / 58.3 / 56.1. Prior: GPT-f 36.6%, HTPS 41.0%, Kimina 80.7%, DeepSeek-Prover-V2 88.9% on miniF2F.
limits: Compute scale is out of reach for us. Geometry excluded. Combinatorics unsolved.
agent_relevance: Extra search time keeps paying (27.9% to 56.1% on Putnam as budget grows). Disproof attempts give free negative signal; a scaffold can also try to refute a candidate lemma before proving.

source: Hubert et al. (2025) AlphaProof at IMO 2024
finding: With AlphaGeometry 2, the system scored 28 of 42 at IMO 2024, one point under gold. AlphaProof solved P1, P2, P6 (algebra and number theory); AlphaGeometry 2 solved P4. Combinatorics P3 and P5 unsolved.
numbers: 28/42 points. Each solved problem needed 2-3 days of TTRL. Problems were formalized by experts after release. For 'find all' problems (P1, P2, P5, P6) hundreds of candidate answers were produced by Gemini 1.5 Pro with Python, and AlphaProof refuted most wrong ones.
limits: Multi-day compute per problem, far above human time limits. Humans did the formalization. Answer guessing relied on a separate LLM.
agent_relevance: Guess many answers, refute the wrong ones by checker, prove the survivor. This is a cheap pattern for S3 with code-checked refutation.

source: Huang & Yang (2025) Winning Gold at IMO 2025 with a Model-Agnostic Verification-and-Refinement Pipeline
finding: Informal (natural-language) proof search with a frozen LLM: generate a solution, self-improve, then a verifier model lists critical errors and justification gaps in a bug report; the model fixes them; repeat until the verifier passes. No Lean.
numbers: Solves 5 of 6 IMO 2025 problems (about 85.7%) with each of Gemini 2.5 Pro, Grok-4 and GPT-5. MathArena best-of-32 baselines on the same problems: 31.6% Gemini 2.5 Pro, 21.4% Grok-4, 38.1% GPT-5. On IMC 2025 (MathArena run): pipeline 94.5% (rank 3 of 434 humans) vs base Gemini 57.7% (rank 92).
quote: Critical errors are seldom missed by the verifier.
limits: The verifier is an LLM, so no formal guarantee. Authors report only qualitative verifier reliability, no measured error rates. Third-party IMC result is for Gemini only.
agent_relevance: Evidence for a verify-and-revise loop with a frozen model, but the checker is the same family of model. Conflicts with our rule that models do not grade themselves; use only with independent checks.

source: Polu & Sutskever (2020); Polu et al. (2022); Lample et al. (2022) - search design across the three systems
finding: Three search schemes compared in the sources: best-first by cumulative log-prob (GPT-f), AlphaZero-like hypertree search with learned value (HTPS), and AND-OR tree search with prove/disprove (AlphaProof). Each step is proposed by a model and ordered or pruned by code.
numbers: miniF2F-test: GPT-f expert iteration 36.6%, HTPS 41.0% (pass@64), both 2022. Metamath: GPT-f 56.2% test, HTPS 61.2% supervised and 65.6% after online training.
limits: Different benchmarks, tactic sets and budgets; cross-paper comparisons are rough.
agent_relevance: The ordering rule is a design slot the program owns. Log-prob ordering is replaceable by a program-computed score such as proof-size or number of open goals.

source: Polu et al. (2022) Formal Mathematics Statement Curriculum Learning - curriculum and transfer findings
finding: Out-of-distribution transfer was initially weak and then appeared as in-distribution performance improved. Adding a curated statement curriculum and synthetic inequalities improved miniF2F beyond the mathlib-only loop. Controls matched attempt counts (a=2).
numbers: Full-curriculum loop used about 33.2k attempts per iteration (25k + 5.6k + 8x327) vs 25k for mathlib-only; a mathlib-only control with a=2 (about 50k attempts) was also plotted as a compute-matched comparison. Appendix F notes the IMO-adapted statements are weaker versions of the originals.
limits: Two IMO problems 'solved' are weakened formal versions. Curriculum was hand picked.
agent_relevance: Training on easy-to-hard problems matters; a scaffold can mimic it by solving easier related lemmas first (decompose) and keeping them as verified context.

source: Jiang et al. (2022) Thor - why premise choice breaks LM provers
finding: A language model has to either memorise a library or be given premises in text. Archive of Formal Proofs has more than 200,000 theorems; 300 premises with definitions can exceed 10,000 characters.
numbers: Steps with premises advance the proof 1.9% of the time vs 28.2% without premises. Success jump 39.0% to 57.0% on PISA once a hammer does premise selection.
quote: We observe that empirically 1.9% of the steps involving premise selection generated by the language model manage to advance the proof
limits: Observed on one fine-tuned Isabelle model.
agent_relevance: A long in-context list of premises is not enough; retrieval by code plus a solver beats asking the model to pick.

source: Yang et al. (2023) LeanDojo - memorization via random splits
finding: Human Lean code has many near-duplicate theorems. A random split lets a model prove test theorems by memorization. The novel_premises split requires at least one premise unseen in training.
numbers: Pass@1 drop from random to novel_premises: tidy 23.8 to 5.3, GPT-4 29.0 to 7.4, ReProver 51.2 to 26.3. BM25 retriever shows a large drop too.
quote: Testing theorems in novel_premises are indeed much more challenging.
limits: Premise novelty is one definition of generalization.
agent_relevance: When we test our agent, we need splits where answers cannot be recalled. Report novel-split numbers.

source: Xin et al. (2024) DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5 - hard exploration in proof search
finding: Proof search is a hard-exploration problem with sparse reward: only a full proof gives reward. RMaxTS adds an intrinsic reward for reaching new tactic states, so search spreads out.
numbers: miniF2F-test: 60.2% single pass; 63.5% with tree search added. ProofNet 22.6% to 25.3%.
quote: the search agent only obtains non-zero rewards when the proof is completely solved
limits: Small gain from search over a strong single-pass sampler: sampling many whole proofs already covers most of what the tree finds.
agent_relevance: Count new verified states as progress. A diversity signal computed by code (new goal states) is a good non-model progress measure.

source: Thakur et al. (2024) COPRA - ablations on information in the prompt
finding: Three kinds of added context are tested: retrieved lemmas, informal proofs, and the search history with error feedback. The agent first runs without retrieval, then restarts with retrieval and informal proofs on unsolved problems to save cost.
numbers: Table 1 (pass counts): few-shot CodeLlama 0.0%, few-shot GPT-3.5 2.8%, COPRA(CodeLlama) 5.73%, COPRA(GPT-3.5) 9.02%, few-shot GPT-4 13.52%; COPRA(GPT-4) solves more than twice few-shot GPT-4 and 29.09% pass@1 on miniF2F-test.
limits: Exact backtracking-off number not extracted in this reading. Contamination caveat for GPT-4.
agent_relevance: The scaffold helps only when the base model is strong enough. A plan for our agent: check the base model's raw pass rate before adding structure.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Goedel-Prover; Xin et al. (2024) DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5 - open-model scaling at fixed budget
finding: On miniF2F, an open 7B prover improved from 50.0% to 57.6% at pass@32 with expert iteration (8 rounds), and stayed ahead at every budget up to thousands of samples.
numbers: Goedel-Prover-SFT 57.6% vs DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5-RL 50.0% at pass@32; Goedel above V1.5 at every budget from pass@32 up to 4x6400 (Figure 1).
limits: Different pass@ definitions across papers (single-pass vs cumulative). Not directly comparable.
agent_relevance: Budget counts: always state attempts per problem when comparing arms.

source: Hubert et al. (2025) AlphaProof - disproof and variant generation as the learning signal
finding: Actors are randomly tasked to prove or disprove each statement. Lean-verified outcomes (proof, disproof or timeout) give grounded feedback. TTRL builds problem variants (for example simplifications) and trains on them for hard targets.
numbers: Gains with TTRL: formal-imo 43.7% (12 TPU-h) to 53.9% (50 TPU-d) to 58.3% (500 TPU-d); PutnamBench 39.4% to 45.5% to 56.1%.
limits: TTRL updates weights at test time; a frozen-model agent cannot do this.
agent_relevance: Frozen analogue: try easier variants of the target in context, keep verified results, then retry the target.

source: Huang & Yang (2025) IMO 2025 pipeline - why single-pass fails
finding: Single-pass generation hits a reasoning-budget wall; iterative review within an LLM verifier raises accuracy. Verifier output separates critical errors from justification gaps, and a human-in-loop step can reject a false report.
numbers: Best-of-32 with self-selection: 21.4% to 38.1% across three models; pipeline: about 85.7% for all three.
quote: General-purpose LLMs are not tailored to solving exceptionally challenging mathematical problems in a single pass.
limits: No ablation of verifier strength or iteration count was quantified in the pages read; model-agnostic claim rests on three models on one contest.
agent_relevance: Typed bug reports (critical vs gap) are a useful format for G2, but the check must be code or an independent model.
